writing.rule: A deployment configuration must fail before the service accepts traffic.
writing.explanation:
A service can compile correctly and still fail because its deployment configuration is wrong. Parse the bind port, database address and operational limits before opening a listener. Report the failed field without echoing a password-bearing connection URL.

This lab accepts decimal ports from 1024 to 65535 and a nonempty database setting containing no whitespace. It rejects signed port syntax, surrounding whitespace and malformed numbers so accepted configuration is predictable. The database check here is intentionally syntactic; it does not prove connectivity, credentials or migration compatibility. The desktop service should perform those separate startup checks and expose readiness only after required initialization. A liveness endpoint and a readiness endpoint answer different operational questions.

The route project is Task Ledger: first keep a reproducible source history, then expose its data through a CLI and HTTP boundary, persist it in SQL, diagnose failures and prepare a release. This lesson owns one contract in that project. Run the worked example before changing the starter and explain which input makes the tempting shortcut fail.

Terminal practice: Start cargo serve --port 8080 --database tasks.db. Refuse an invalid port, then check /health after successful startup.

The compiler lab is independent of the reading question. Edit solution.rs; the app supplies a separate caller with normal, empty and adversarial inputs. A successful unchanged demonstration does not prove your implementation. After the lab, apply the same contract to the route companion project. Its README separates the on-device adapter from the desktop Cargo/TCP profile.

writing.task: Accept an ASCII-digit decimal port in 1024..=65535 and a nonempty database string without whitespace. Return port for port errors and database for database errors; validate the port first. Keep the public signature. Open the compiler lab and edit solution.rs; do not edit the private verification caller.
writing.success: The separate caller accepts the changed solution and rejects unchanged TODO, a wrong implementation and a printed success message.
writing.question: What does accepting a database configuration string prove?
answers: That every future request will succeed
writing.feedback: Configuration parsing, connectivity and readiness are separate checks.

recall.question: With ports allowed from 1024 to 65535, why are `"+8080"`, `"65536"` and `"0"` all rejected, and why check for ASCII digits before parsing?
recall.answer: `"+8080".parse::<u16>()` would succeed, so the digit check is what enforces the no-sign grammar; 65536 does not fit `u16`; 0 is below 1024. All return `Err("port")` before any listener opens.

recall.question: How do liveness and readiness endpoints differ, and what does a syntactic database-setting check not prove?
recall.answer: Liveness says the process is running; readiness says required initialization has finished and it can take traffic. A syntax check proves nothing about connectivity, credentials or migration compatibility, which need separate startup checks.
